summary: Sets out requirements for a Media Server Control Protocol that lets an application server use a media server. It covers services such as announcements, interactive voice response, and conferencing. The document says the logical roles existed in IETF work but the protocol between them had not been defined. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Think of a manager telling a sound-and-video helper to play a message or mix a call. This paper lists what a language between them needs.

questions: application server to media server protocol
what is a media server control protocol
what is an application server vs media server
subtitle: What a protocol must do so an application server can direct a media server to play, mix and collect audio and video.

tldr.problem: IETF conferencing work describes an application server and a media server as separate logical entities, but nothing defined the protocol between them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists 32 numbered requirements (REQ-MCP-01 to REQ-MCP-32) for a Media Server Control Protocol covering media control, mixing, interactive voice response and operations.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a protocol. It leaves the details of security and the protocol itself to the framework and protocol documents.

today: RFC 5167 is an Informational RFC from March 2008, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements only and does not define the protocol itself.

sections.title: Introduction and Roles
sections.content:
The conferencing framework in RFC 4353 describes several functional entities but does not specify the protocols between them. RFC 5167 sets out requirements for a protocol that lets an Application Server (AS) work with one or more Media Servers (MS).

The AS hosts instances of a communication application and may include the conference policy server, the notification server and the focus. The MS provides real-time media processing: it includes the mixer, plays announcements, detects DTMF, transcodes, and may record streams for IVR functions. An optional Media Resource Broker (MRB) collects and supplies media server information.

The requirements cover the protocol only, not AS or MS functionality. Since the media server is a centralized component, the working group charter says it will not investigate distributed media processing algorithms or control protocols.
sections.eli5: One helper decides what should happen on a call, and another helper does the actual sound and picture work. They need a way to talk.

sections.title: General Media Control Requirements
sections.content:
The control protocol must let one or more application servers request services from one or more media servers over a reliable transport. It must support conferencing and Interactive Voice Response (IVR), with media types including audio, tones, text and video. A media resource broker or proxy may exist but must not be required.

On the control channel there are requests to the MS, responses from the MS, and notifications to the AS. SIP/SDP is to be used to establish and modify media connections. Other requirements say it should be possible to span one conference across multiple media servers, to split call legs away from a main conference without re-establishing them, and that the protocol should be extensible with forward and backward compatibility.

The AS must be able to mute and control gain, play specific announcements to a single user or a whole mix, create, delete and manipulate mixing, IVR or announcement sessions, and ask for a session summary report. The MS must be able to notify the AS of events in the media stream when asked.
sections.eli5: The manager can say play this sound, turn that person down, or start a new little room, and the helper answers or taps the manager on the shoulder when something happens.

sections.title: Mixing, IVR and Operational Requirements
sections.content:
For mixing, the AS defines a conference mix, at conference or user level, and may define a custom video layout of rectangular sub-windows and map streams to them. The MS must tell the AS which layouts it supports and who the active sources are, such as the active speaker, who may differ from the video source. The protocol should let the AS ask the MS to record a conference mix.

For IVR, the AS must be able to instruct the MS to run IVR scripts, held on a server or carried in the control message, and receive results. In the AS-managed style, the AS plays announcements, gets responses such as DTMF, and decides the next phase. The AS should also be able to have the MS record a short participant stream and play it back, which the RFC says is not a recording requirement.

Operationally, the AS must be able to audit MS state during an active session, and the MS must be able to report its status.
sections.eli5: The manager can arrange who appears where on a video call, run a phone menu such as press 1 for sales, and check on the helper at any time.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Several numbered requirements deal with security. The protocol must include authentication so only an authorized AS can talk to the MS and vice versa, and it must use transport protection for confidentiality and integrity. Different application servers may have different privileges, and the protocol should prevent unauthorized operations. Because several ASs may control one MS, resources used by one AS must be protected from another.

The security section adds that all operations need to be authorized, with the MS governed by authorization rules from AS/MS policy. Normal SIP mechanisms, including Digest authentication and certificates as in RFC 3261, can be used. Details are left to the framework and protocol documents.
sections.eli5: Only the right manager may boss the helper around, and one manager must not mess up another manager's work.
